content: Spasticity is a significant health issue for individuals with spinal cord injuries (SCI). It restricts their mobility and diminishes their ability to perform daily activities and maintain independence. Additionally, spasticity can lead to pain, reduced range of motion, contractures, sleep disturbances, and impaired walking ability, particularly in patients with incomplete spinal cord lesions. The effectiveness of currently available pharmacological treatments for spasticity remains uncertain, and these medications may also cause adverse effects. Evaluating the efficacy of these treatments is further complicated by the lack of reliable and valid measurement tools. The purpose of this systematic review was to critically evaluate and summarize the existing evidence on the effectiveness of available pharmacological treatments for spasticity in SCI patients. It also aimed to identify areas where further research is necessary. Specifically, the review sought to assess the effectiveness and safety of drugs such as baclofen, dantrolene, tizanidine, and others, as well as to evaluate the safety and efficacy of different methods of administering baclofen. To gather relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Injuries Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE/PubMed, EMBASE, Zetoc, Web of Knowledge, CINAHL, and Current Controlled Trials. Reference lists of relevant papers were also reviewed to identify additional studies. The search was last updated in July 2008. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with either parallel or cross-over designs that involved SCI patients experiencing severe spasticity. Studies were excluded if less than 50% of the participants had a spinal cord injury. Two investigators independently assessed the methodological quality of the included studies, considering factors such as allocation concealment, blinding, patient characteristics, inclusion and exclusion criteria, interventions, outcomes, and losses to follow-up. Due to heterogeneity among the studies, a quantitative synthesis of the results was not possible. Nine studies met the inclusion criteria. Of these, eight were cross-over trials, and one was a parallel-group trial. Two studies, involving a total of 14 SCI patients, demonstrated that intrathecal baclofen significantly reduced spasticity, as measured by the Ashworth Score and improvements in activities of daily living (ADL), compared to placebo. Importantly, no adverse effects were reported in these studies. Another study, which compared tizanidine to placebo in 118 SCI patients, found that tizanidine significantly improved the Ashworth Score but did not lead to improvements in ADL performance. However, the tizanidine group experienced notable adverse effects, including drowsiness and dry mouth (xerostomia). For other drugs, such as gabapentin, clonidine, diazepam, amytal, and oral baclofen, the evidence did not support clinically significant effectiveness in treating spasticity. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to guide clinicians in making informed decisions about antispastic treatment for SCI patients. They emphasized the urgent need for further research to strengthen the scientific foundation for managing spasticity in this patient population.
